metadata.title: Efficient Decision-Making by Volume-Conserving Physical Object

extraction_notes.note: The letter has no section headings (only an unnumbered Acknowledgement), so every node has section null.
The label eq:cond1 is defined twice (on the second line of (5)-(6) and on (7)); it is never referenced, so no edge depends on it.
Apparent typos kept verbatim: E(S)=(mu_A+mu_B)N should be a difference, and N_N stands for N_B in N = N_A + N_N.
Table 1 (estimates of each reward probability when gamma is known) is a float and has no node; DP8 depends on it through 'From the above estimates'.
The Chernoff bound Q(x) <= exp(-x^2/2)/2 is stated inline in the same sentence that names the regret, so it gets no separate theorem node; it is part of DP12.
DP4 is one 'Here, ...' sentence introducing five symbols and cannot be split below a sentence; phi and phi_T are defined in 'where' sentences kept inside the result nodes ClP11 and ClP15.
TOW dynamics is the authors' earlier algorithm (cited kim1-kim6) restated here; marked external, though the letter's contribution is its analysis.

metadata.extraction_comment: Results are physics-style derivations (CLT/Gaussian approximations, heuristic separation conditions) rather than proved theorems; derived quantities are kept as equation and claim nodes.

nodes.name: M slot machines
nodes.statement: Suppose there are $M$ slot machines, each of which returns a reward; for example, a coin, with a certain probability that is unknown to a player.

nodes.name: reward probabilities P_A, P_B
nodes.statement: Let us consider a minimal case: two machines A and B give rewards with individual probabilities $P_A$ and $P_B$, respectively.

nodes.name: multi-armed bandit problem (MBP)
nodes.statement: The player makes a decision on which machine to play at each trial, trying to maximize the total reward obtained after repeating several trials. The multi-armed bandit problem (MBP) is used to determine the optimal strategy for finding the machine with the highest reward probability as accurately and quickly as possible by referring to past experiences.
nodes.statement_short: Two-armed bandit: find the machine with the highest reward probability accurately and quickly while maximizing total reward.

nodes.name: displacement X_k
nodes.statement: Here, the variable $X_k$ represents the displacement of terminal $k$ from an initial position, where $k\in \{A,B\}$.

nodes.name: Tug-of-war (TOW) dynamics
nodes.statement: If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$. In TOW dynamics, the MBP is represented in its inverse form: instead of ``rewarding'' the player when machine $k$ produces a coin with a probability $P_k$, we ``punish'' the player when the machine gives no coin with a probability $1 - P_k$. In this respect, the displacement $X_A$ ($= - X_B$) is determined by the following equations: \begin{eqnarray} X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray} Here, $Q_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$, $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played, $L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$, $\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected, and $\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter. Eq.(\ref{eq:org}), called the ``learning rule'', reflects the volume-conservation law. Consequently the TOW dynamics evolve according to a particularly simple rule: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}).
nodes.statement_short: Volume-conserving tug-of-war: play the machine with the larger displacement $X_k=Q_A-Q_B+\delta$, adding $+1$ on reward and $-\omega$ on no reward.

nodes.name: decision rule
nodes.statement: If $X_k$ is a maximum, we assume that the body makes a decision to play machine $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Play the machine whose terminal displacement is maximal.

nodes.name: inverse (punishment) form
nodes.statement: In TOW dynamics, the MBP is represented in its inverse form: instead of ``rewarding'' the player when machine $k$ produces a coin with a probability $P_k$, we ``punish'' the player when the machine gives no coin with a probability $1 - P_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Represent the MBP inversely: punish on no-reward rather than reward.

nodes.name: displacement update
nodes.statement: In this respect, the displacement $X_A$ ($= - X_B$) is determined by the following equations: \begin{eqnarray} X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Compute $X_A=Q_A-Q_B+\delta$ with $Q_k=N_k-(1+\omega)L_k$.

nodes.name: per-trial increment rule
nodes.statement: Consequently the TOW dynamics evolve according to a particularly simple rule: in addition to the fluctuation, if machine $k$ is played at each time $t$, $+1$ and $-\omega$ are added to $X_k(t-1)$ when rewarded and non-rewarded, respectively (Fig.~\ref{fig:stow}).
nodes.statement_short: Add $+1$ or $-\omega$ to $X_k$ when machine $k$ is rewarded or not.

nodes.name: TOW displacement and learning rule equations
nodes.statement: X_A(t) & = & Q_A(t) - Q_B(t) + \delta(t) ,\\ Q_k(t) & = & N_k - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}L_k .
nodes.label: diffe

nodes.name: estimate Q_k, counts N_k, L_k, fluctuation delta, weight omega
nodes.statement: Here, $Q_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is an ``estimate'' of information on past experiences accumulated from the initial time $1$ to current time $t$, $N_k$ counts the number of times that machine $k$ has been played, $L_k$ counts the number of punishments when playing machine $k$, $\delta(t)$ is an arbitrary fluctuation to which the body is subjected, and $\omega$ is a weighting parameter to be described in detail later on in this Letter.
nodes.statement_short: $Q_k$ is the accumulated estimate, $N_k$ plays, $L_k$ punishments, $\delta$ a fluctuation, $\omega$ a weighting parameter.

nodes.name: learning rule
nodes.statement: Eq.(\ref{eq:org}), called the ``learning rule'', reflects the volume-conservation law.

nodes.name: random-walk flight parameters alpha, beta
nodes.statement: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(a), $\alpha$ (right flight when rewarded) and $\beta$ (left flight when non-rewarded) are the parameters.

nodes.name: P_A > P_B
nodes.statement: We assume that $P_A$ $>$ $P_B$ for simplicity.

nodes.name: random-walk displacement R_k
nodes.statement: After time step $t$, the displacement $R_k(t)$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) can be described by \begin{eqnarray} R_k(t) & = & \alpha (N_k - L_k) - \beta \hspace{1mm}L_k \nonumber \\ & = & \alpha N_k - (\alpha + \beta)\hspace{1mm}L_k . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Random-walk displacement $R_k=\alpha N_k-(\alpha+\beta)L_k$.

nodes.name: random-walk displacement
nodes.statement: R_k(t) & = & \alpha (N_k - L_k) - \beta \hspace{1mm}L_k \nonumber \\ & = & \alpha N_k - (\alpha + \beta)\hspace{1mm}L_k .
nodes.label: eq:ran

nodes.name: expected random-walk displacement
nodes.statement: E( R_k(t) ) = \{\alpha P_k - \beta (1 - P_k)\}\hspace{1mm} N_k .
nodes.statement_short: Expected displacement is $\{\alpha P_k-\beta(1-P_k)\}N_k$.

nodes.name: sign conditions for correct judgment
nodes.statement: \alpha P_A - \beta (1 - P_A) & > & 0 , \\ \alpha P_B - \beta (1 - P_B) & < & 0 .
nodes.label: eq:cond1

nodes.name: parameter condition P_B < beta/(alpha+beta) < P_A
nodes.statement: P_B < \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} < P_A .
nodes.label: eq:cond1

nodes.name: fixed-point choice of beta/(alpha+beta)
nodes.statement: We can easily confirm that the following form satisfies the above conditions: \begin{equation} \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2} . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choosing $\beta/(\alpha+\beta)=(P_A+P_B)/2$ satisfies the separation conditions.

nodes.name: midpoint choice
nodes.statement: \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta} = \frac{P_A + P_B}{2} .
nodes.label: eq:fixed

nodes.name: omega = beta/alpha
nodes.statement: From $R_k(t)/\alpha $ $=$ $Q_k(t)$, we obtain $\omega = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$.

nodes.name: derivation of omega_0
nodes.statement: From this and Eq.(\ref{eq:fixed}), we obtain \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma}{2 - \gamma} , \\ \gamma & = & P_A + P_B . \end{eqnarray} Here, we have set the parameter $\omega$ to $\omega_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct substitution: combine $\omega=\beta/\alpha$ with the midpoint condition to get $\omega_0=\gamma/(2-\gamma)$.

nodes.name: nearly optimal weighting parameter omega_0
nodes.statement: \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma}{2 - \gamma} , \\ \gamma & = & P_A + P_B .
nodes.statement_short: $\omega_0=\gamma/(2-\gamma)$ with $\gamma=P_A+P_B$.
nodes.label: eq:w0

nodes.name: TOW with omega_0 solves the MBP
nodes.statement: Therefore, we can conclude that the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$ can solve the MBP correctly.
assumptions: the algorithm using the learning rule $Q_k$ with the parameter $\omega_0$

nodes.name: imaginary system with known gamma
nodes.statement: In many popular algorithms such as the $\epsilon$-greedy algorithm, at each time $t$, an estimate of reward probability is updated for either of the two machines being played. On the other hand, in an imaginary circumstance in which the sum of the reward probabilities $\gamma$ $=$ $P_A$ $+$ $P_B$ is known to the player, we can update both of the two estimates simultaneously, even though only one of the machines was played.
nodes.statement_short: If $\gamma=P_A+P_B$ were known, both machines' estimates could be updated after each play.

nodes.name: expected rewards Q'_k of the imaginary system
nodes.statement: From the above estimates, each expected reward $Q^{\prime}_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) is given as follows: \begin{eqnarray} Q^{\prime}_A & = & N_A \hspace{1mm} \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} + N_B \hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \bigr) \nonumber \\ & = & N_A - L_A + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_B + L_B, \\ Q^{\prime}_B & = & N_A\hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} \bigr) + N_B\hspace{1mm} \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \nonumber \\ & = & N_B - L_B + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_A + L_A. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Expected rewards combining direct and $\gamma$-inferred estimates for both machines.

nodes.name: expected rewards Q'_A, Q'_B
nodes.statement: Q^{\prime}_A & = & N_A \hspace{1mm} \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} + N_B \hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \bigr) \nonumber \\ & = & N_A - L_A + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_B + L_B, \\ Q^{\prime}_B & = & N_A\hspace{1mm} \bigl( \gamma \hspace{1mm} - \frac{N_A - L_A}{N_A} \bigr) + N_B\hspace{1mm} \frac{N_B - L_B}{N_B} \nonumber \\ & = & N_B - L_B + (\gamma - 1) \hspace{1mm} N_A + L_A.
nodes.label: eq:qAp

nodes.name: TOW estimate difference Q_A - Q_B
nodes.statement: Q_A - Q_B = (N_A - N_B) - (1 + \omega)\hspace{1mm}(L_A - L_B).
nodes.label: eq:dq

nodes.name: rescaled rewards Q''_j
nodes.statement: When we transform the expected rewards $Q^{\prime}_j$s into $Q^{\prime \prime}_j = Q^{\prime}_j / (2 - \gamma)$, we can obtain the difference \begin{equation} Q^{\prime \prime}_A - Q^{\prime \prime}_B = (N_A - N_B) - \frac{2}{2-\gamma} \hspace{1mm} (L_A - L_B). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rescale $Q''_j=Q'_j/(2-\gamma)$ and take the difference.

nodes.name: rescaled imaginary-system difference
nodes.statement: Q^{\prime \prime}_A - Q^{\prime \prime}_B = (N_A - N_B) - \frac{2}{2-\gamma} \hspace{1mm} (L_A - L_B).
nodes.label: eq:dqpp

nodes.name: coefficient matching at omega_0
nodes.statement: Comparing the coefficients of Eq.(\ref{eq:dq}) and (\ref{eq:dqpp}), the differences in their constituent terms are always equal when $\omega=\omega_0$ (Eq.(\ref{eq:w0})) is satisfied.
conclusions: the differences in their constituent terms are always equal
nodes.statement_short: At $\omega=\omega_0$ the TOW difference equals the imaginary-system difference.

nodes.name: TOW learning rule equivalent to the imaginary system
nodes.statement: This derivation implies that the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously. In other words, TOW dynamics imitates the imaginary system that determines its next move at time $t+1$ in referring to the estimates of the two machines, even if one of them was not actually played at time $t$.
conclusions: the learning rule for TOW dynamics is equivalent to that of the imaginary system in which both of the two estimates can be updated simultaneously

nodes.name: origin of TOW high performance
nodes.statement: This unique feature in the learning rule, derived from the fact that the sum of reward probabilities is given in advance, may be one of the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics.

nodes.name: Monte Carlo: omega_0 near-peak performance
nodes.statement: Monte Carlo simulations were performed it was verified that TOW dynamics with $\omega_0$ exhibits an exceptionally high performance, which is comparable to its peak performance---achieved with the optimal parameter $\omega_{opt}$.
conclusions: TOW dynamics with $\omega_0$ exhibits an exceptionally high performance, which is comparable to its peak performance

nodes.name: omega_0 for M-machine case
nodes.statement: To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine, as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:random}(b), all we need is the following $\omega_0$: \begin{eqnarray} \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma^{\prime}}{2 - \gamma^{\prime}} , \\ \gamma^{\prime} & = & P_{(m)} + P_{(m+1)} \end{eqnarray} Here, $P_{(m)}$ denotes the top $m$-th reward probability.
assumptions: To separate distributions of the top $m$-th and top $(m+1)$-th machine
nodes.statement_short: For $M$ machines, use $\omega_0=\gamma'/(2-\gamma')$ with $\gamma'$ the sum of the $m$-th and $(m+1)$-th top probabilities.

nodes.name: M-machine omega_0
nodes.statement: \omega_0 & = & \frac{\gamma^{\prime}}{2 - \gamma^{\prime}} , \\ \gamma^{\prime} & = & P_{(m)} + P_{(m+1)}

nodes.name: cheater algorithm
nodes.statement: To further investigate the origins of the high performance of TOW dynamics, let us consider another imaginary model for solving the MBP, called the ``cheater algorithm.'' The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray} Here, $X_{k, i}$ is a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded). If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$. If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary algorithm that observes both machines each step and plays the one with the larger reward sum $S_k$.

nodes.name: compute reward sums
nodes.statement: The cheater algorithm selects a machine to play according to the following estimate $S_k$ ($k\in \{A,B\}$) \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N} , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N} . \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Sum the observed rewards $S_k$ of each machine over $N$ steps.

nodes.name: play A if S_A > S_B
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $>$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, machine $A$ is played at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: play B if S_B > S_A
nodes.statement: If $S_B$ $>$ $S_A$ at time $t=N$, machine $B$ is played at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: random tie-break
nodes.statement: If $S_A$ $=$ $S_B$ at time $t=N$, a machine is played randomly at time $t=N+1$.

nodes.name: why the algorithm cheats
nodes.statement: Note that the algorithm refers to results of both machines at time $t$ without any attention to which machine was played at time $t-1$. In other words, the algorithm ``cheats'' because it plays both machines and collects both results, but declares that it plays only one machine at a time.

nodes.name: mean and variance mu_k, sigma_k^2
nodes.statement: The expected value and the variance of $X_k$ are defined as $E (X_k) = \mu_k $ and $V (X_k) = \sigma_k^{2}$. Here, $\mu_k$ is the same as the $P_k$ defined earlier.

nodes.name: Gaussian approximation of S_k
nodes.statement: From the central-limit theorem, $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k) = \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k) = \sigma_k^{2} N$.
conclusions: $S_k$ has a Gaussian distribution with $E (S_k)  =  \mu_k N$ and $V (S_k)  =  \sigma_k^{2} N$

nodes.name: moments of S = S_A - S_B (cheater)
nodes.statement: If we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$, $S$ has a Gaussian distribution and carries the following values: \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & (\mu_A + \mu_B) N ,\\ V (S) & = & (\sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}) N ,\\ \sigma (S) & = & \sqrt{ \sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}} \sqrt{N} . \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: If we define a new variable $S = S_A - S_B$
conclusions: $S$ has a Gaussian distribution and carries the following values:
nodes.statement_short: $S=S_A-S_B$ is Gaussian with mean and variance linear in $N$.

nodes.name: moments of S (cheater)
nodes.statement: E (S) & = & (\mu_A + \mu_B) N ,\\ V (S) & = & (\sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}) N ,\\ \sigma (S) & = & \sqrt{ \sigma_A^{2} + \sigma_B^{2}} \sqrt{N} .

nodes.name: probability of playing the worse machine
nodes.statement: From Fig.~\ref{fig:Qfunc}, the probability of playing machine $B$, which has a lower reward probability, can be described as {\bf Q}$(\frac{E(S)}{\sigma(S)})$.
conclusions: the probability of playing machine $B$, which has a lower reward probability, can be described as {\bf Q}$(\frac{E(S)}{\sigma(S)})$

nodes.name: Q-function
nodes.statement: Here, {\bf Q}$(x)$ is a {\bf Q}-function.

nodes.name: cheater error probability Q(phi sqrt N)
nodes.statement: We obtain \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi \sqrt{N}) . \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi = \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The cheater plays the worse machine at time $N+1$ with probability $Q(\phi\sqrt N)$.

nodes.name: cheater error probability
nodes.statement: P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi \sqrt{N}) .

nodes.name: regret
nodes.statement: Using the Chernoff bound ${\bf Q}(x) \leq \frac{1}{2} \exp(-\frac{x^2}{2})$, we can calculate the upper bound of a measure, called the ``regret'', which quantifies the accumulated losses of the cheater algorithm. \begin{equation} regret = (\mu_A - \mu_B) E(N_B). \end{equation}
differentia: quantifies the accumulated losses of the cheater algorithm
nodes.statement_short: Regret $=(\mu_A-\mu_B)E(N_B)$, bounded via the Chernoff bound $Q(x)\le\frac12 e^{-x^2/2}$.

nodes.name: regret formula
nodes.statement: regret = (\mu_A - \mu_B) E(N_B).

nodes.name: cheater regret upper bound
nodes.statement:
E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} { f Q}(\phi \sqrt{t}) 
onumber \ & \leq & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1}  rac{1}{2} \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2} t) 
onumber \ & = &  rac{1}{2} + \Sigma_{t=1}^{N-1}  rac{1}{2} \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2} t) 
onumber \ & \leq &  rac{1}{2} + \int_{0}^{N-1}  rac{1}{2} \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2} t) dt 
onumber \ & = &  rac{1}{2} -  rac{1}{\phi^2} \left( \exp(- rac{\phi^2}{2}(N-1)) - 1 ight) \ & ightarrow &  rac{1}{2} +  rac{1}{\phi^2} .
nodes.statement_short: $E(N_B)\le\frac12+\frac1{\phi^2}$ via the Chernoff bound and a sum-to-integral comparison.

nodes.name: constant regret of the cheater algorithm
nodes.statement: Note that the regret becomes constant as $N$ increases.
conclusions: the regret becomes constant as $N$ increases

nodes.name: TOW reward sums S_A, S_B
nodes.statement: In this case, \begin{eqnarray} S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N_A} - \omega L_A , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N_B} - \omega L_B . \end{eqnarray} $X_{k, i}$ is also a random variable that takes either $1$ (rewarded) or $0$ (non-rewarded).
nodes.statement_short: TOW estimate sums: rewards minus $\omega L_k$.

nodes.name: TOW reward sums
nodes.statement: S_A & = & X_{A, 1} + X_{A, 2}, + \cdots + X_{A, N_A} - \omega L_A , \\ S_B & = & X_{B, 1} + X_{B, 2}, + \cdots + X_{B, N_B} - \omega L_B .

nodes.name: L_k = (1 - mu_k) N_k
nodes.statement: Here, we use $L_k$$=$$(1 - \mu_k) N_k$.

nodes.name: moments of S_k for TOW
nodes.statement: Then, we obtain $E (S_k) = \{ \mu_k - (1 - \mu_k) \omega \} N_k$ and $V (S_k) = \sigma_k^{2} N_k$.

nodes.name: moments of S for TOW in terms of N and D
nodes.statement: Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$, we also obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) N + \nonumber \\ & & \{ \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) - \omega \} D ,\\ V (S) & = & \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2} N + \frac{\sigma_A^2 - \sigma_B^2}{2} D . \end{eqnarray}
assumptions: Using the new variables $S = S_A - S_B$, $N = N_A + N_N$, and $D = N_A - N_N$
conclusions: E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) N + \nonumber \\ & & \{ \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) - \omega \} D ,\\ V (S) & = & \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2} N + \frac{\sigma_A^2 - \sigma_B^2}{2} D .

nodes.name: TOW moments of S
nodes.statement: E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) N + \nonumber \\ & & \{ \frac{\mu_A + \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega) - \omega \} D ,\\ V (S) & = & \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2}{2} N + \frac{\sigma_A^2 - \sigma_B^2}{2} D .

nodes.name: TOW error probability Q(phi_T sqrt N)
nodes.statement: If the conditions $\omega = \omega_0$ and $\sigma_A = \sigma_B$ $\equiv \sigma$ are satisfied, we then obtain \begin{eqnarray} E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega_0) N ,\\ V (S) & = & {\sigma^2} N , \end{eqnarray} and \begin{eqnarray} P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{N}) . \end{eqnarray} Here, $\phi_{T} = \frac{(\mu_A - \mu_B) (1 + \omega_0)}{2 \sigma}$.
nodes.statement_short: With $\omega=\omega_0$ and equal variances, TOW plays the worse machine with probability $Q(\phi_T\sqrt N)$.

nodes.name: TOW moments at omega_0
nodes.statement: E (S) & = & \frac{\mu_A - \mu_B}{2} (1 + \omega_0) N ,\\ V (S) & = & {\sigma^2} N ,

nodes.name: TOW error probability
nodes.statement: P(t=N+1,B) & = & {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{N}) .

nodes.name: TOW regret upper bound
nodes.statement: E(N_B) & = & \Sigma_{t=0}^{N-1} {\bf Q}(\phi_{T} \sqrt{t}) \nonumber \\ & \leq & \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} \left( \exp(-\frac{\phi_{T}^2}{2}(N-1)) - 1 \right) \\ & \rightarrow & \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\phi_{T}^2} .
nodes.statement_short: $E(N_B)\le\frac12+1/\phi_T^2$ for TOW dynamics.

nodes.name: constant regret of TOW dynamics
nodes.statement: Note that the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases.
conclusions: the regret for TOW dynamics also becomes constant as $N$ increases

nodes.name: logarithmic regret of optimal MBP algorithms (Auer et al.)
nodes.statement: It is known that optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al., have a regret proportional to $\log(N)$.
assumptions: optimal algorithms for the MBP, defined by Auer et al.

nodes.name: constant vs logarithmic regret
nodes.statement: The regret has no finite upper bound as $N$ increases because it continues to require playing the lower-reward machine to ensure that the probability of incorrect judgment goes to zero. A constant regret means that the probability of incorrect judgment remains non-zero in TOW dynamics, although this probability is nearly equal to zero. However, it would appear that the reward probabilities change frequently in actual decision-making situations, and their long-term behavior is not crucial for many practical purposes. For this reason, TOW dynamics would be more suited to real-world applications.
nodes.statement_short: Log regret drives error probability to zero; TOW's constant regret leaves a tiny nonzero error but suits changing environments.
